To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
prescribed burning did not result in the same spider community structure as wildfire, but did increase spider richness in the long term.

1) species richness and composition was affected by disturbance and differed among seasons, and 2) disturbance-tolerant and disturbance-generalist species were more prevalent in treated areas, whereas disturbance-specialists were more prevalent in controls.

(1) the spider community in the EMEND study area has a relatively high species richness; (2) species richness is lower in burned and harvested plots than in control plots; (3) the spider community is relatively stable in harvested and burned plots; (4) species turnover is higher in control plots than in harvested and burned sites; and (5) species richness and turnover are lower in burned than in harvested plots.

prescribed fire is not an effective surrogate for wildfire in this forest type.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
prescribed post-harvester burning is not a good substitute for natural fire disturbance.
prescribed post-harvet fire did not emulate natural wildfire in the boreal forest.
prescribed burning may be useful to retain biodiversity in the short term but may not emulate the natural disturbance paradigm.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the EMEND experiment is an excellent opportunity to study how disturbance regimes affect the spider communities in the boreal forest.
the effects of fire and harvest may be more subtle and longer term than previously thought.

the EMEND experiment is a valuable platform to assess the effects of disturbance on biodiversity, and that the effects of harvesting, burning, and their interaction on biodiversity will be more fully understood as the experiment progresses.
